nameStory: This petite plant gets its name from its distinctive leaves, which are shaped like a lyre - that ancient harp-like instrument. The deeply lobed leaves with their rounded bottom section and narrower top reminded botanists of the curved, musical instrument. The 'rockcress' part comes from its love of growing in rocky, sandy places where many other plants can't take hold.
description: Lyreleaf rockcress is a small, delicate wildflower that rarely grows taller than your hand. This member of the mustard family forms low rosettes of deeply-lobed leaves close to the ground, with slender stems rising up to display tiny white flowers. Despite its petite size, it's a hardy little plant that thrives in challenging rocky habitats where bigger plants struggle. You'll need to look carefully to spot this modest beauty, as it easily blends into its surroundings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The rosette leaves are deeply lobed like a lyre or fiddle, with a broad rounded section at the bottom and narrower lobes above. They feel slightly fuzzy to the touch and have a fresh, slightly peppery mustard-family scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, typical of the mustard family. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across and clustered at the tips of thin, wiry stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading rosettes that hug the ground, with flowering stems that rise only a few inches high. The whole plant has a delicate, wispy appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops narrow, upright seed pods (siliques) that split open to release tiny seeds. The pods are slender and stand erect on the flowering stems.

habitat: Look for lyreleaf rockcress in sandy, rocky places like exposed ledges, gravelly shores, and thin-soiled areas where competition from larger plants is minimal. In New England, it's quite rare and typically found in naturally disturbed sites with well-drained, nutrient-poor soils. It often grows alongside other hardy plants that can tolerate harsh, exposed conditions.

seasonality.spring: Rosette leaves emerge early and the distinctive lyre-shaped foliage is most noticeable. Small white flowers begin appearing in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny white cross-shaped flowers on thin stems. Seed pods begin developing after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open. Basal rosettes may persist and remain visible if conditions aren't too harsh.
seasonality.winter: Usually dies back to ground level, though rosettes may survive mild winters in protected spots.

funFact: This humble little plant is actually a close cousin of one of the most famous plants in science - Arabidopsis thaliana, which was the first plant to have its entire genome sequenced and is used in labs worldwide to unlock the secrets of how plants grow and develop!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its relative mouse-ear cress, but lyreleaf rockcress has much more deeply lobed, lyre-shaped leaves compared to mouse-ear cress's simple, oval leaves. Memory trick: 'Lyre' has deeply lobed leaves like the curves of the musical instrument.
contextualKnowledge: With only 29 recorded observations in all of New England, this is one of our rarer native wildflowers. Its scarcity makes every sighting special, so if you find one, consider reporting it to local botanists or iNaturalist to help track this uncommon species.
compareHints: Compared to its famous relative mouse-ear cress, lyreleaf rockcress has much more dramatically lobed leaves and tends to grow in rockier, more exposed habitats. While mouse-ear cress often grows as a garden weed in disturbed soil, lyreleaf rockcress seeks out the challenging rocky places that most plants avoid. Both share the same tiny white four-petaled flowers and belong to the mustard family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mouse-ear cress differs from its relative lyreleaf rockcress by being much smaller and having simple, oval leaves rather than lobed or toothed ones.
